concepts.title: Negative numbers
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: A negative is an amount below zero — temperatures, debt, depths. The rules that matter: subtracting a negative adds (5 − (−3) = 8), multiplying two negatives makes a positive ((−2) × (−3) = 6), and one negative makes a negative. Picture a number line: adding moves right, subtracting moves left.

misconceptions.name: Sign slip with negatives
misconceptions.pattern: Treats minus signs as decoration: 5 − (−3) becomes 2, and (−2) × (−3) becomes −6.

items.prompt: Work out (-4) × (-5).
items.explanation: Two negatives multiply to a POSITIVE: (-4) × (-5) = 20. The opposite of the opposite is the original direction.

items.prompt: Work out 7 − (-8).
items.explanation: Subtracting a negative is ADDING: 7 − (-8) = 7 + 8 = 15. Taking away a debt leaves you richer.

items.prompt: Work out (-4) × (-2).
items.explanation: Two negatives multiply to a POSITIVE: (-4) × (-2) = 8. The opposite of the opposite is the original direction.

items.prompt: Work out 3 − (-6).
items.explanation: Subtracting a negative is ADDING: 3 − (-6) = 3 + 6 = 9. Taking away a debt leaves you richer.

items.prompt: Work out 4 − (-3).
items.explanation: Subtracting a negative is ADDING: 4 − (-3) = 4 + 3 = 7. Taking away a debt leaves you richer.

items.prompt: Work out 6 − (-9).
items.explanation: Subtracting a negative is ADDING: 6 − (-9) = 6 + 9 = 15. Taking away a debt leaves you richer.

concepts.title: Order of operations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Brackets, then Indices/Exponents, then Division and Multiplication left to right, then Addition and Subtraction left to right (BIDMAS/PEMDAS). 3 + 4 × 2 = 3 + 8 = 11, not 14 — multiplication always acts first. The convention exists so everyone in the world reads one expression the same way.

items.prompt: Work out 5 + 2 × 2.
items.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition: 2 × 2 = 4 first, then 5 + 4 = 9. Working left to right gives 14, which is wrong.

items.prompt: Work out 7 + 9 × 7.
items.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition: 9 × 7 = 63 first, then 7 + 63 = 70. Working left to right gives 112, which is wrong.

items.prompt: Work out 2 + 9 × 4.

items.prompt: Work out 3 + 5 × 6.

items.prompt: Work out 9 + 6 × 9.

items.prompt: Work out 5 + 5 × 6.

concepts.title: Algebraic expressions
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: A letter holds a place for a number: 3x + 2 means 'three of something, plus two'. Collecting like terms simplifies: 3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2y stays put. Expanding brackets multiplies every term inside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Substitution replaces letters with values: if x = −2, then 3x + 2 = −4.

items.prompt: Evaluate 5x² − 2x when x = 6.
items.explanation: Square first, then multiply: 5(6²) = 180, minus 2(6) = 12. So 180 − 12 = 168.

items.prompt: Evaluate 5x² − 4x when x = 2.
items.explanation: Square first, then multiply: 5(2²) = 20, minus 4(2) = 8. So 20 − 8 = 12.

items.prompt: Evaluate 2x² − 2x when x = 3.
items.explanation: Square first, then multiply: 2(3²) = 18, minus 2(3) = 6. So 18 − 6 = 12.

items.prompt: Evaluate 6x² − 3x when x = 4.
items.explanation: Square first, then multiply: 6(4²) = 96, minus 3(4) = 12. So 96 − 12 = 84.

items.prompt: Evaluate 5x² − 3x when x = 6.

items.prompt: Evaluate 6x² − 4x when x = 4.

concepts.title: Coordinates & graphs
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: A coordinate pair (3, −2) pinpoints a location: 3 right, 2 down from the origin. The x-axis runs horizontally, y vertically. Plotting an equation's points and joining them reveals its shape — lines for linear, parabolas for quadratics. Graphs turn algebra into geometry you can see.

items.prompt: How far is the point (−4, 2) from the origin (0, 0)?
items.explanation: Distance from the origin is Pythagoras: d = √(x² + y²) = √(-4² + 2²) = √20. Adding |x| + |y| measures the staircase walk, not the straight line.

concepts.title: Index laws
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: a³ means a × a × a. Multiplying powers with the same base adds the indices: a² × a³ = a⁵. Dividing subtracts them: a⁵ ÷ a² = a³. A power of zero gives 1 (a⁰ = 1) because dividing aⁿ by aⁿ must give 1. Negative indices flip into a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a². Fractional indices are roots: a^(1/2) = √a.

misconceptions.name: Misreads negative indices
misconceptions.pattern: Treats a⁻² as a negative number instead of 1/a².

items.prompt: Work out (4^2)².
items.explanation: A power of a power MULTIPLIES the indices: (4^2)² = 4^4 = 256.

items.prompt: Work out (3^3)².
items.explanation: A power of a power MULTIPLIES the indices: (3^3)² = 3^6 = 729.

items.prompt: Work out (3^2)².
items.explanation: A power of a power MULTIPLIES the indices: (3^2)² = 3^4 = 81.

items.prompt: Work out (2^3)².
items.explanation: A power of a power MULTIPLIES the indices: (2^3)² = 2^6 = 64.

items.prompt:
Folding a sheet of paper in half doubles its thickness each time.
· 0 folds: 0.2 mm
· 1 fold: 0.4 mm
· 2 folds: 0.8 mm
After 10 folds, the thickness is how many times the thickness with no folds?
items.explanation: Each fold DOUBLES the thickness, so after 10 folds it has doubled 10 times: 2^10 = 1024 times. That is exponential: 10 lots of 2 (20) is a straight line and 10² (100) is a square, and both grow far more slowly than doubling.

concepts.title: Linear equations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Solve 3x + 5 = 20 by undoing operations in reverse order: subtract 5 (3x = 15), divide by 3 (x = 5). Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — the equation is a balance. Two-step, brackets, unknowns on both sides (5x = 2x + 9) all reduce to the same discipline.

misconceptions.name: Breaks the balance when solving
misconceptions.pattern: Adds to one side only: 3x + 5 = 20 becomes 3x = 25.

items.prompt: Solve 3(x + 2) = 30.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: x + 2 = 10, so x = 8. (Expanding first works too: 3x + 6 = 30.)

items.prompt: Solve 6(x + 5) = 60.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 6: x + 5 = 10, so x = 5. (Expanding first works too: 6x + 30 = 60.)

items.prompt: Solve 3(x + 1) = 9.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: x + 1 = 3, so x = 2. (Expanding first works too: 3x + 3 = 9.)

items.prompt: Solve 4(x + 1) = 12.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 4: x + 1 = 3, so x = 2. (Expanding first works too: 4x + 4 = 12.)

items.prompt: Solve 3(x + 2) = 18.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: x + 2 = 6, so x = 4. (Expanding first works too: 3x + 6 = 18.)

items.prompt: Solve 3(x + 5) = 27.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: x + 5 = 9, so x = 4. (Expanding first works too: 3x + 15 = 27.)

items.prompt: Solve 2(x − 3) = x + 0.
items.explanation: Expand the bracket first: 2x − 6 = x + 0. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 1x and adding 6 to BOTH sides — gives 1x = 6, so x = 6 ÷ 1 = 6. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

Expand the bracket first: 5x − 35 = 4x − 24. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 4x and adding 35 to BOTH sides — gives 1x = 11, so x = 11 ÷ 1 = 11. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

items.prompt: Solve 4(x − 2) = x + 28.
items.explanation: Expand the bracket first: 4x − 8 = x + 28. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 1x and adding 8 to BOTH sides — gives 3x = 36, so x = 36 ÷ 3 = 12. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

items.prompt: Solve 2(x − 2) = x − 1.
items.explanation: Expand the bracket first: 2x − 4 = x − 1. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 1x and adding 4 to BOTH sides — gives 1x = 3, so x = 3 ÷ 1 = 3. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

items.prompt: Solve 4(x − 5) = x + 7.
items.explanation: Expand the bracket first: 4x − 20 = x + 7. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 1x and adding 20 to BOTH sides — gives 3x = 27, so x = 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

items.prompt: Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 6.
items.explanation: Expand the bracket first: 3x − 6 = 2x + 6. Collect the x-terms on both sides — subtracting 2x and adding 6 to BOTH sides — gives 1x = 12, so x = 12 ÷ 1 = 12. Doing any of that to one side only is the balance error: an equation is a scale, so every move happens twice.

concepts.title: Expanding & factorising
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Expand: (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 5x + 6 — every term meets every term. Factorising reverses it: x² + 5x + 6 seeks two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: (x + 2)(x + 3). The difference of two squares is a shortcut: x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3). These skills are the grammar of every later algebra topic.

misconceptions.name: Sign error when expanding
misconceptions.pattern: (x − 3)(x + 2) becomes x² + 5x − 6 — the minus doesn't distribute.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 5)(x + 8). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: The x-terms are 5x + 8x = 13x, so b = 13. (And c = 5 × 8 = 40.)

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + 4)(x + 2).
items.explanation: x² + 2x + 4x + 8 = x² + 6x + 8. Every term carries its sign.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 9)(x + 8). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: The x-terms are 9x + 8x = 17x, so b = 17. (And c = 9 × 8 = 72.)

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + -5)(x + 1).
items.explanation: x² + 1x + -5x + -5 = x² − 4x − 5. Every term carries its sign.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + 5)(x + 1).
items.explanation: x² + 1x + 5x + 5 = x² + 6x + 5. Every term carries its sign.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 8)(x + 9). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: The x-terms are 8x + 9x = 17x, so b = 17. (And c = 8 × 9 = 72.)

items.prompt: Expand (2x + 6)(x + 4). The result is 2x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: The x-terms come from 2x × 4 and 6 × x: 8x + 6x = 14x, so b = 14.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 13x + 42) cm² and its width is (x + 6) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 13x + 42 = (x + 6)(x + 7), because 6 × 7 = 42 and 6 + 7 = 13. Dividing by the width (x + 6) leaves (x + 7) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 8x + 15) cm² and its width is (x + 5) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 8x + 15 = (x + 5)(x + 3), because 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 + 3 = 8. Dividing by the width (x + 5) leaves (x + 3) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 9x + 18) cm² and its width is (x + 6) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 9x + 18 = (x + 6)(x + 3), because 6 × 3 = 18 and 6 + 3 = 9. Dividing by the width (x + 6) leaves (x + 3) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt:
Expand and simplify (2x + 7)(4x − 4).

What is the coefficient of x in the expansion?
items.explanation: The x-term is the sum of the two CROSS products: the outer pair 2x × -4 = -8x, and the inner pair 7 × 4x = 28x. Adding them: -8 + 28 → the coefficient is 20. Stopping at -8 forgets the inner pair, and 28 forgets the outer one — the two halves of the same step. 8 is the coefficient of x², and -28 is the constant.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 7x + 12) cm² and its width is (x + 3) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), because 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7. Dividing by the width (x + 3) leaves (x + 4) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

concepts.title: Straight line graphs
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (rise over run — how much y grows per unit of x) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. Parallel lines share m; perpendicular lines multiply to −1. From two points, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Every real-world rate — speed, cost per item, fuel use — is a gradient.

misconceptions.name: Gradient upside-down or sign-flipped
misconceptions.pattern: Computes run over rise, or drops the minus on a downhill line.

items.prompt: A line has equation y = 4x + 5. What is y when x = 6?
A line has equation y = 3x + 1. What is y when x = 1?
items.explanation: Substitute: y = 3(1) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.

items.prompt: A line has equation y = 4x − 3. What is y when x = 3?
items.explanation: Substitute: y = 4(3) − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9.

items.prompt: A line has equation y = 5x − 5. What is y when x = 3?
A line has equation y = 1x + 0. What is y when x = 4?
items.explanation: Substitute: y = 1(4) + 0 = 4 + 0 = 4.

items.prompt: A line has equation y = 1x + 6. What is y when x = 6?
items.explanation: Substitute: y = 1(6) + 6 = 6 + 6 = 12.

items.prompt:
A straight line passes through (4, -30) and (5, -33).

Work out the coordinates of the point where the line crosses the x-axis.
items.explanation: Three steps, and the third is the one asked for. Gradient: (-33 − -30) ÷ (5 − 4) = -3 ÷ 1 = -3. Intercept: at (4, -30), -30 = -3 × 4 + c, so c = -18. Root: the line crosses the x-axis where y = 0, so 0 = -3x − 18, giving x = -6. The point is (-6, 0). Answering (0, -18) is where the line crosses the Y-axis — the same shape of question about the other axis.

items.prompt:
A straight line passes through (4, 0) and (5, -3).

Work out the coordinates of the point where the line crosses the x-axis.
items.explanation: Three steps, and the third is the one asked for. Gradient: (-3 − 0) ÷ (5 − 4) = -3 ÷ 1 = -3. Intercept: at (4, 0), 0 = -3 × 4 + c, so c = 12. Root: the line crosses the x-axis where y = 0, so 0 = -3x + 12, giving x = 4. The point is (4, 0). Answering (0, 12) is where the line crosses the Y-axis — the same shape of question about the other axis.

items.prompt: A water tank holds 60 litres. Water is added at a steady 2 litres per minute. A graph of volume (y litres) against time (x minutes) is a straight line. How much water is in the tank after 14 minutes?
items.explanation: The line is y = 2x + 60: the gradient 2 is the change per minute and 60 is the volume at x = 0, the intercept. After 14 minutes: 2 × 14 + 60 = 88 litres. Answering 28 reports the water ADDED rather than the water in the tank — the intercept dropped because it was never written down.

items.prompt: A water tank holds 57 litres. Water is added at a steady 6 litres per minute. A graph of volume (y litres) against time (x minutes) is a straight line. How much water is in the tank after 5 minutes?
items.explanation: The line is y = 6x + 57: the gradient 6 is the change per minute and 57 is the volume at x = 0, the intercept. After 5 minutes: 6 × 5 + 57 = 87 litres. Answering 30 reports the water ADDED rather than the water in the tank — the intercept dropped because it was never written down.

concepts.title: Completing the square
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4: halve the x coefficient, square it, adjust. This form exposes the vertex (−3, −4) instantly, shows the minimum/maximum value, and solves equations by isolating a perfect square. It is also how the quadratic formula is derived — completing the square on the general equation.

misconceptions.name: Completing the square: forgets the constant
misconceptions.pattern: x² + 6x + 5 becomes (x + 3)² without subtracting the added 9.

items.prompt: Express x² + 10x + 21 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 5, so the square is (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25; the expression has 21 there instead, so it is (x + 5)² − 4 = (x + 5)² − 4. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 5)² = 0 — that is x = -5, and the minimum value is -4. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -5.

items.prompt: Write x² + 2x + 6 in the form (x + p)² + q. What is q?
items.explanation: Halve the x coefficient: p = 1, so (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1. The constant was 6, so q = 6 − 1 = 5. Forgetting to subtract the added 1 is the classic error.

items.prompt: Express x² + 14x + 57 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 7, so the square is (x + 7)² = x² + 14x + 49; the expression has 57 there instead, so it is (x + 7)² + 8 = (x + 7)² + 8. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 7)² = 0 — that is x = -7, and the minimum value is 8. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -7.

items.prompt: Express x² + 16x + 58 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 8, so the square is (x + 8)² = x² + 16x + 64; the expression has 58 there instead, so it is (x + 8)² − 6 = (x + 8)² − 6. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 8)² = 0 — that is x = -8, and the minimum value is -6. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -8.

items.prompt: Express x² + 6x + 3 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 3, so the square is (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; the expression has 3 there instead, so it is (x + 3)² − 6 = (x + 3)² − 6. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 3)² = 0 — that is x = -3, and the minimum value is -6. items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 3, so the square is (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; the expression has 1 there instead, so it is (x + 3)² − 8 = (x + 3)² − 8. concepts.title: Quadratic equations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Quadratics can have two, one, or no real solutions — visible as where the parabola cuts the x-axis. Solve by factorising (x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → (x−2)(x−3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3), by completing the square, or by the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many solutions exist before you solve.

misconceptions.name: Loses a root when solving quadratics
misconceptions.pattern: Divides by x instead of factorising, or takes only one ± branch.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 9x + 18 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: Factorise: (x − 3)(x − 6) = 0, so x = 3 or x = 6. The smaller root is 3.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 8x + 15 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: Factorise: (x − 5)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 5 or x = 3. The smaller root is 3.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 6x + 5 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: Factorise: (x − 5)(x − 1) = 0, so x = 5 or x = 1. The smaller root is 1.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 9x + 20 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: Factorise: (x − 4)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 5. The smaller root is 4.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 6x + 8 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: Factorise: (x − 2)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 4. The smaller root is 2.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − 5x + 6 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5 are 3 and 2, giving (x − 3)(x − 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = 2 OR x = 3 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² + x − 30 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² + 1x − 30 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -30 and add to 1 are 5 and -6, giving (x − 5)(x + 6) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -6 OR x = 5 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − 2x − 24 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 2x − 24 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -24 and add to -2 are 6 and -4, giving (x − 6)(x + 4) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -4 OR x = 6 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − x − 20 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 1x − 20 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -20 and add to -1 are -4 and 5, giving (x + 4)(x − 5) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -4 OR x = 5 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − 6x + 8 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 6x + 8 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to 8 and add to -6 are 4 and 2, giving (x − 4)(x − 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = 2 OR x = 4 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² + x − 2 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² + 1x − 2 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -2 and add to 1 are 1 and -2, giving (x − 1)(x + 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -2 OR x = 1 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

concepts.title: Surds
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: √2 cannot be written exactly as a fraction — its decimal never repeats. A surd is an exact root like √2, √3, √5. Simplify using √(ab) = √a × √b: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Rationalise denominators by multiplying top and bottom by the surd (or its conjugate for expressions like 1/(1+√2)). Surds keep answers exact where decimals only approximate.

items.prompt: Simplify √50.
items.explanation: √50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Take the largest perfect-square factor first.

items.prompt: Simplify √48.
items.explanation: √48 = √(16 × 3) = √16 × √3 = 4√3. Take the largest perfect-square factor first.

items.prompt: Simplify √32.
items.explanation: √32 = √(16 × 2) = √16 × √2 = 4√2. Take the largest perfect-square factor first.

items.prompt: Simplify √20.
items.explanation: √20 = √(4 × 5) = √4 × √5 = 2√5. Take the largest perfect-square factor first.

items.prompt: Simplify √8.
items.explanation: √8 = √(4 × 2) = √4 × √2 = 2√2. Take the largest perfect-square factor first.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify: (4√3 + 2)(4√3 − 2).
items.explanation: This is the difference of two squares: (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B². Here A = 4√3 and B = 2, so A² = 16×3 = 48 and B² = 4, giving 48 − 4 = 44. Note the √3 does NOT survive: squaring the surd term is what removes it, and that is why this expansion is the standard way to rationalise a surd denominator.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify: (2√6 + 4)(2√6 − 4).
items.explanation: This is the difference of two squares: (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B². Here A = 2√6 and B = 4, so A² = 4×6 = 24 and B² = 16, giving 24 − 16 = 8. Note the √6 does NOT survive: squaring the surd term is what removes it, and that is why this expansion is the standard way to rationalise a surd denominator.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify: (2√2 + 5)(2√2 − 5).
items.explanation: This is the difference of two squares: (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B². Here A = 2√2 and B = 5, so A² = 4×2 = 8 and B² = 25, giving 8 − 25 = -17. Note the √2 does NOT survive: squaring the surd term is what removes it, and that is why this expansion is the standard way to rationalise a surd denominator.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify: (5√3 + 3)(5√3 − 3).
items.explanation: This is the difference of two squares: (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B². Here A = 5√3 and B = 3, so A² = 25×3 = 75 and B² = 9, giving 75 − 9 = 66. Note the √3 does NOT survive: squaring the surd term is what removes it, and that is why this expansion is the standard way to rationalise a surd denominator.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify: (4√6 + 6)(4√6 − 6).
items.explanation: This is the difference of two squares: (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B². Here A = 4√6 and B = 6, so A² = 16×6 = 96 and B² = 36, giving 96 − 36 = 60. Note the √6 does NOT survive: squaring the surd term is what removes it, and that is why this expansion is the standard way to rationalise a surd denominator.

items.prompt: Simplify fully: (√45 + √20) ÷ √5.
items.explanation: No surd here is in its simplest form, and none can be combined until it is: √45 = √(3²×5) = 3√5 and √20 = √(2²×5) = 2√5. Now they are like surds: (3√5 + 2√5) ÷ √5 = 5√5 ÷ √5, and the √5 cancels, leaving 5. Adding 45 + 20 under one root is the slip this question is built to catch — √a + √b is not √(a + b).
